what_it_does: Macro placement is an early step in chip design where large, pre-built blocks of circuitry — called macros (think of them as prefabricated rooms, such as a memory bank or a processor core) — are positioned on the chip's floor plan before finer-grained wiring begins. Poor placement lengthens wires, slows signals, and hurts the final chip's speed. Expert human designers tend to push macros toward the chip's edges so that the interior is free for the dense wiring that connects them. ReMaP automates this by first placing macros along an ellipse using an angle-based analytical method, which naturally spreads them toward the periphery while also respecting how data flows between them. A second step then snaps macros to the actual chip boundary, mimicking expert practice. The process is applied recursively — refining the arrangement in multiple passes — and an automatic parameter-tuning step searches for the best settings for each design.
